scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Marfa was introduced to Hyderabad State in the 18th century by the Siddi community, who were of East African descent and served as cavalry guards for the Asaf Jahi Nizams.
The Nizams, claiming Arab ancestry, patronized the music, which was adapted from the Afro-Arab traditions of Hadhramawt, Yemen.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Marfa is a traditional sign of welcome and a staple of Hyderabadi Muslim weddings.
It serves as a celebratory expression of identity for the Siddi and Hadhrami diaspora in India.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves 'jiggling' and rhythmic movements performed with janbiya daggers, talwars (swords), or latts (canes).
It is based on the tempo of the music, with both men and women participating in the dancing, though only men typically play the instruments.
Watch for Weapon Jiggling.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (odxM6gSikJY)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Group performance, often in open celebratory spaces

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is played at a high tempo using marfa (kettledrums), daff, dhol, sticks, steel pots (handi), and wooden strips called thapi.
The vocal meter and chorus effects are set according to specific rhythmic beats known as 'teen maar taal'.
Listen for the marfa (kettledrum), daff, dhol, sticks.
The pulse is 4/4 or 2/4 at about 140 beats a minute.
A high-tempo, percussive sound dominated by the sharp strike of wooden thapi and the metallic resonance of steel pots, layered over deep kettledrum beats.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers often carry traditional weapons like the janbiya or talwar.
The dance is performed in public squares, at weddings, and officially at the Red Fort in New Delhi during national holidays.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Asaf Jahi Nizams are the primary historical patrons who integrated Marfa into official state ceremonies and celebrations.
Variants are defined by specific rhythmic patterns such as sewari, bamb sheklah, and jumbali zimbali, which reflect different influences within the Afro-Arab diaspora.
Marfa is likely derived from the Yemeni Bar'a dance and was brought to India by the Siddi and Hadhrami diaspora.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
